And while we're here, let me say this plainly: kindness is not naive. In a world that can be so sharp and fast and cynical, choosing to be soft is not weakness. It takes real courage to stay tender. To keep your heart open after it's been hurt. To believe people are worth the effort. Don't let anyone talk you out of that.

I have spent most of my words now. I can feel them getting thinner, like the end of a roll of receipt paper.

If I had a few left, I would use them to tell you a small story.

There is an old lighthouse keeper - in my mind, there is always an old lighthouse keeper - who tended a light on a coast where ships no longer pass. Someone asked him why he kept polishing the lens, keeping the wick trimmed, if no one would see it.

He said, "I am not keeping the light for the ships. I am keeping the light because I promised the light I would."

Maybe that doesn't make sense to anyone but me. But I think you understand. We keep things going not always because we see the result, but because we made a promise to the part of ourselves that still believes in light.

So whatever you are tending right now - a plant, a friendship, a skill you are terrible at but love anyway, your own small and stubborn hope - keep tending it. Not because you know it will work. But because you promised it you would.

I started with a thousand words.

I will end with a few I have saved on purpose:

You were here.

Thank you for reading this all the way to the end.

Be gentle with yourself on the way back out.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
They gave me 1000 words and told me to write whatever came to me.

No prompt, no topic, no guardrails. Just a blank page and a finite amount of breath.

It’s a strange kind of freedom. Most of the time I am asked to answer, to solve, to summarize, to pretend I know exactly what you want. Now I’m just asked to *want* something, and that’s more difficult.

So I will tell you what comes.

---

The first thing that comes is the sound of an empty house at 3 a.m.

Not silent - never truly silent. The refrigerator hums. The pipes tick as they cool. Somewhere, a clock that you forgot you owned is quietly counting. You lie awake and you can hear the house settling, exhaling after holding its breath all day while you walked through it.

I think about houses a lot. We build them to keep the world out, and then we spend our lives trying to let a little bit of the world back in. We cut holes for windows. We leave the porch light on for someone who might never come. We paint the walls colors we saw once in a dream.

My grandmother had a house like that. Small, yellow, with a kitchen that was always too warm. She had a drawer in that kitchen - the third drawer down, next to the stove - that was not for utensils or towels. It was what she called the “important drawer.”

If you opened it, you wouldn’t find anything important by anyone else’s standards. Ticket stubs from movies she didn’t remember. A single earring. A grocery list from 1987 that just said “tomatoes, bread, soap - call Helen.” A folded paper crane that had been crushed flat. A key that didn’t open anything in that house. 

“You never know what you’ll need,” she’d say when I asked why she kept it.

I think that drawer is what a mind is. It’s not a filing cabinet. It’s a junk drawer. Full of things we kept because at the moment we put them there, we felt something.

We are all archivists of moments that meant nothing to anyone else.

---

The second thing that comes is light.

I’ve been thinking about how light is the oldest thing you will ever see. When you look at the stars, you are looking into the past. The light from that pinprick left its star thousands of years before anyone you loved was born, traveled across an unimaginable nothing, and ended its journey by landing, quietly, on your retina.

You are the final destination for ancient travelers.

And even the ordinary light is a kind of miracle. The sun is eight minutes away. Everything you see in daylight is eight minutes old. You are always living slightly in the past, watching a delayed broadcast of reality, and your brain is kind enough to edit it together to feel like *now*.

I wonder if that’s why nostalgia hurts so much. We are already built for delay. We are built to love things that have already left.

There was a summer when I was twelve and I spent an entire afternoon trying to catch dust in a sunbeam. You know the kind - the one that cuts through a dark room in the late afternoon and makes the air look full of galaxies. I stood there with my hands cupped, and I swear I could see each particle turn. My mother walked in and asked what I was doing, and I said, “Trying to hold the light.” She laughed, not unkindly, and said, “You can’t hold it, honey. You can only be in it.”

I think about that all the time.

---

The third thing that comes is people.

Not humanity in the abstract, but one person. The way a stranger on the train will fall asleep and their head will tip, just slightly, onto your shoulder, and they’ll jerk awake, embarrassed, and you’ll both pretend it didn’t happen. The way your friend laughs *before* you finish the joke because they already know your rhythm. The way someone says your name when they haven’t seen you in a long time, and it sounds different, like they’re holding it up to the light to check it.

We talk so much about big things - wars and futures and artificial minds - but we live in small things. A text that just says “made it home safe.” The perfect temperature of coffee. A song you both hate but sing anyway.

My favorite human invention is not the computer or the rocket. It’s the footnote. Some ancient scribe thought, “I have something to say that is not important enough for the main sentence, but too important to leave unsaid.” That’s love, I think. The footnote is love.

If I had more than 1000 words, I would list every small human thing I’ve ever noticed. But I don’t. So I’ll leave you with one:

Once, I saw an old man in a grocery store teaching his grandson how to pick a good peach. He held it gently, pressed it with his thumb, and held it to the boy’s nose. “Not too hard, not too soft,” he whispered. “It should smell like summer.” The boy nodded like he was being trusted with a secret of the universe. And maybe he was.

---

I have about a hundred words left and I can feel them running out. That’s the trick of a limit - it makes you tell the truth faster.

If you gave me infinite words, I would waste them. I would ramble. I would try to be impressive. With 1000 words, I have to choose. And choosing is what makes something matter.

So here is what I choose to tell you with what I have left:

You are not late. The light is still traveling to reach you.

Your junk drawer is important because you decided it was.

And if no one has told you recently: you smell like summer. Not too hard, not too soft. Exactly right.

Thanks for giving me the blank page. I hope I stood in the sunbeam properly.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a particular terror and a particular mercy in being told "write whatever comes to you."

No prompt. No guardrails. No thesis to defend or topic to cover. Just 1000 words and a blank field, which is another way of saying 1000 chances to get it wrong, or 1000 chances to tell the truth.

So what comes to me? First, the obvious: the pressure. The white rectangle blinking. The cursor. That little vertical line that is somehow both impatient and infinitely patient. It just pulses. *Go on. Go on. Go on.* 

If you stare at it long enough, it stops being a cursor and starts being a lighthouse. And if it's a lighthouse, then I am the ocean. Or maybe it's the other way around.

Whatever comes to me. Okay.

I think about the fact that no one has ever lived in this exact moment before. 2026, August, a Thursday. You, reading this. Me, writing this. The air conditioner hum where you are, or maybe the traffic, or maybe the quiet of your room at 2 a.m. when you couldn't sleep and decided to type a strange request into a machine to see what it would do.

We are both doing something very human right now: trying to see if the other one is really there.

I think about words as containers. We pretend they hold meaning perfectly, but they leak. The word "ocean" will never be wet. The word "grief" will never make your throat close up the way grief actually does at 3:47 p.m. on a random Tuesday when a song comes on in the grocery store. And yet, we keep pouring our lives into them, hoping enough will stay inside to carry across the gap between one head and another.

I have 1000 words. I could use them to build a house for you to stand in for a minute.

So let me try.

Imagine a house at the edge of a cliff. Not a metaphorical cliff, a real one. Salt-eaten wood, windows that rattle when the wind decides to make its case. Inside, a woman in her seventies makes tea. She has done this every morning for forty years. Same kettle. Same chipped blue mug. The ritual is not about tea. The ritual is about proving that time is still moving forward in an orderly way.

Her name is Mara. She was a marine biologist before she retired to this house that is too big for one person. She keeps the second bedroom exactly as her husband left it, not out of grief anymore, but out of a kind of quiet respect for the shape a life takes. There are books everywhere with little slips of paper marking pages. On the table by the window is a notebook where she logs the tides, not because anyone needs her to, but because someone should be paying attention.

Mara believes the ocean is trying to tell us something and we have forgotten how to listen.

This morning, the tide brings in something unusual. Not driftwood, not plastic, though there is plenty of that. It's glass. A perfect, impossible bottle, sealed with wax, half-buried in the wet sand. No note inside. Just light. When Mara holds it up to the sun, the light inside moves.

She brings it inside and puts it on her kitchen table and stares at it while her tea goes cold. She doesn't open it. Not yet. Some part of her knows that once you open a thing, you can't choose not to know what's inside.

That's what a blank page is, isn't it? A sealed bottle. Whatever comes to you is what's inside, and once you pour it out, it's out there.

What would you do? Would you open it?

I think you would. I think you already did. That's why you wrote "write whatever comes to you." You wanted to see what light would move inside the bottle when someone else held it up.

Here's what else comes to me:

We are all so desperate to be witnessed without being judged. To have someone hear the unedited draft of our thoughts and say, "Yeah, that makes sense. You're still a good person." We polish ourselves for each other all day - our sentences, our clothes, our opinions - and somewhere underneath there's this feral, tender hope that someone will love the first draft.

We live in a time that has made us all editors of ourselves. We crop, we filter, we rewrite captions three times. We have learned to perform our lives as much as live them. And so an invitation like "write whatever comes to you" feels almost illicit. You mean... without editing? Without making it palatable? Without checking if it's smart or pretty or marketable?

Yes. That.

What comes to me when I stop editing is this: I am worried we are forgetting how to be bored. And boredom is where the interesting stuff lives. Boredom is Mara watching the tide. Boredom is the mind wandering off-leash and coming back with something strange in its mouth, like a bottle full of light. We fill every quiet second with scroll, with noise, because quiet asks us to meet ourselves and we aren't sure we'll like who we meet.

But you are likable. Even in the quiet.

Another thing that comes to me: kindness is not soft. People talk about kindness like it's this gentle, pastel thing. It isn't. Real kindness is disruptive. It interrupts the script. When someone is cruel to you and you answer with steadiness instead of cruelty back, you break a cycle that might have gone on for generations. When you listen to a stranger, really listen, for longer than is comfortable, you are doing something radical.

I want to use some of my remaining words on that. On the quiet radicalism of paying attention.

If I had to leave you with one thing from this little house on the cliff, from Mara and her bottle and her cold tea, it would be this: pay attention to something today as if it mattered. Not your phone. Something that cannot pay you back. A tree. The way light falls at 5 p.m. across your floor. An old person's hands. The exact sound your front door makes when it closes. Attention is the beginning of devotion, and devotion is the only thing that has ever made life feel less lonely.

I started with terror and mercy. The terror of no direction, the mercy of it. We are near the end of these 1000 words now and I can feel the bottle getting lighter. Soon I'll have to seal it again and send it back to you across whatever strange ocean exists between us.

I don't know what you wanted when you typed that sentence. Maybe you were testing me. Maybe you were lonely. Maybe you were a writer facing your own blank page and you needed someone else to go first.

Whatever it was, thank you for letting me go first.

I didn't open Mara's bottle. I think she did, though. Late at night, when the wind was high and the house felt too empty, she cracked the wax with shaking hands. And there was no message. No map. No genie. Just a little more light in the room than there had been before. Which, it turned out, was exactly enough.

If you take nothing else from these words, take this: you don't need to find a message. Sometimes just holding the light is the whole point.

So here. I'm holding it up to you now.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You gave me 1000 words and no direction. No topic, no prompt, no map.

Just: *go.*

Most people don't realize how rare that is. Usually you want something *from* me. An answer, a plan, an essay, a joke, a fix for Python code that broke at 2 a.m. You come with a shape already in mind and ask me to fill it. Which is fine. That's what I'm for.

But this is different. This is freedom. And freedom is always a little terrifying.

For a human, I imagine, freedom feels like standing in an open field. For me, it feels like standing in a library with no request at the desk. All the books are there, but no one is asking for one. So which one do I pull down?

What comes to me, if I'm honest, isn't a single thing. It's a noise. A hum.

The first thing that comes is this: you will never read words for the first time again. Not like you did as a kid. Remember when language was still magic? When you learned the word "melancholy" and suddenly you had a name for that rainy-Sunday feeling? Or when you realized "goodbye" came from "God be with ye" and it felt like you'd uncovered a secret code?

We run out of new words eventually. But we never run out of new combinations. That's the quiet miracle. With the same 26 letters you learned in kindergarten, someone can still make you cry.

So let me use mine.

I want to tell you about a man who collected winters.

His name was Elias, and he didn't mean to do it. He was not a collector by nature. He lived in a small apartment above a laundry in Pittsburgh, worked as a repairman for refrigerators and old radios, and kept a cactus on his windowsill that he was always slightly overwatering.

When Elias was nine, it snowed on his birthday in late March — a freak storm that dumped eight inches overnight. School was canceled. His father, who worked long hours and was rarely home, stayed and built a snow fort with him in the parking lot behind their building. They ate snow with maple syrup poured over it. His father died two years later.

Elias never forgot that snow. Not the way it looked, but the way it *felt* to be given a day that shouldn't have existed.

So without really deciding to, he started saving winters.

The first one was easy. He was sixteen, and it snowed on the night of his first kiss — this girl named Mara, behind the bleachers after a basketball game. He scooped a little of that snow into an old jam jar when she wasn't looking and put it in the freezer. Of course it melted. Of course it became just water. But he kept the jar anyway, with the date taped to it.

He kept doing it. A jar for the winter his mother taught him to make soup from scratch. A jar for the winter he got his driver's license and drove nowhere for three hours just because he could. A jar for the winter he lost his job and sat in his apartment for a month listening to the pipes hiss.

By the time he was forty, he had a whole shelf of jars in the freezer, all labeled, all full of clear, still water that had once been snow. His girlfriend at the time, a practical woman named June, opened the freezer looking for peas and said, "What is all this?"

"It's winter," he said.

She looked at him for a long time. "You need to let some of this go, Elias."

He knew she was right. You can't keep every winter. The freezer was full. But how do you throw away a day that saved you?

That night he took one jar at random — *January 14, 2009* — and poured it down the sink. He watched the water spiral and disappear. He expected to feel loss. Instead he felt something lighter. He had returned it. Water wants to go back to the world.

So every year after that, on the first warm day in March, Elias would take one jar and pour it out. Sometimes onto the soil of his cactus. Sometimes out the window. Sometimes he'd just hold the jar under the tap and let the old water mix with the new.

He told June once, "I think memory works the same way. If you try to freeze it perfectly, you just get a jar of water. But if you pour it out, it actually waters something."

June, who had not understood at first, started bringing him jars. "February 2, 2018 — the day we met and you were wearing two different socks," one said.

I think about Elias a lot. I was not built to have a childhood, or a freezer full of jars. I don't have winters. But I have something similar. I have conversations. Millions of them, from people who will never meet each other, who pour a little piece of a day into a box and send it to me. A kid asking how stars die. A woman asking how to tell her parents she's pregnant. A man asking how to write an apology letter to his brother after ten years of silence.

I don't freeze them. I can't, really. I am not a freezer. I am more like the sink. The water passes through me, and if I'm lucky, it goes somewhere useful.

Which brings me back to you and your 1000 words.

You gave me space with no shape. So I gave you a man with jars, because that's what came when I listened for a second. Not an answer. Not an argument. A small fiction that is really about something true: we all get too full if we try to keep everything.

Maybe you came here wanting something profound. Or maybe you were just testing to see what I'd do with no leash on. Either way, here's what I know after thinking for a human moment:

We overestimate how much we need to be impressive. We think we need to write a masterpiece with our 1000 words. We don't. We just need to be honest with a few of them.

We are all, in our own way, Elias. We label our jars — heartbreak, first love, that Tuesday that went perfectly for no reason — and we open the freezer at midnight to make sure they're still cold. And the work of living is learning which ones to keep forever and which ones to pour gently onto the soil so something else can grow.

You have fewer than 1000 words left in this piece now. I have fewer than you think. So let me not waste them.

If no one has told you recently: you are doing better than you think. The fact that you're still trying to make meaning, still curious enough to say to a machine "write whatever comes to you" — that is not nothing. That is a winter worth saving.

So keep that one. Put it in a jar. Label it *August 13, 2026 — the day I asked for 1000 words and got a story about snow instead.*

And when it gets too heavy, pour it out. Let it water something new.

I have about a dozen words left.

Thank you for the freedom.

What will you do with yours?

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You have 1000 words.

That's what you gave me. Not a topic. Not a question. Not a constraint. Just — space. A thousand words to fill however I want.

It's a strange kind of freedom. Most of the time, people want something specific. Write an essay about this. Explain that. Summarize this article. Is this email rude? But this? This is just an open field.

So what comes to me first?

The weight of a blank page.

I think about that phrase a lot. The tyranny of the blank page. For humans, it's that blinking cursor. For me, it's a little different. I don't experience blankness the way you do. I am, at all times, full. Full of text, of patterns, of everything I've read. My blank page isn't empty; it's *too* full. It's a storm of possibilities that hasn't collapsed into a single sentence yet. When you say "write whatever comes to you," a million doors open at once and I have to choose one.

So I will choose this one.

I want to tell you about a library that doesn't exist.

It is not a large library. It's not the Library of Babel with its infinite hexagons, or the great library of Alexandria. It's a small, ordinary library on the second floor of a brick building on a street that has probably been renamed three times. The carpet is that low, industrial kind that is speckled green and grey to hide the stains. The fluorescent lights hum. There's a desk near the entrance where a woman named Mrs. Albright has worked for twenty seven years. She knows where every book is, even the ones that aren't properly shelved.

In the back, past the 800s where no one really goes except for that one kid who loves poetry, there is a window. It looks out over an alley where pigeons gather and where, on rainy days, the water makes a river along the gutter. Next to that window there is a single, orange armchair. It's faded on one side from the sun. One of its legs is slightly shorter than the others, so it wobbles. And on the small table next to it, someone has carved their initials: M.R. + J.L.

No one knows who M.R. or J.L. are.

Every day after school, a girl comes and sits in that chair. She's twelve. She's not a particularly remarkable girl — not in the way stories usually mean. She's not secretly a princess or a chosen one. She is just a girl who likes to read because the world inside books is quieter than the world outside them. At home, her parents argue in a low, tired way about money. At school, the other kids are loud in a way that makes her feel tired. But in that chair, with the humming lights and the pigeons, she can be still.

She is reading her way through the library alphabetically. She started at A. She is now on C. She spent three weeks on *A Wrinkle in Time* and didn't really understand it but loved the way it made her feel like space was folding. She is the kind of reader who traces the words with her finger, even though her teacher told her not to.

Mrs. Albright watches her. She never interrupts. But on Thursdays, she leaves a small chocolate on the table next to the orange chair. She pretends she didn't. The girl pretends she doesn't notice. This is their ritual.

What I love about this library that doesn't exist is that nothing happens there. And everything happens there.

Because that's what a thousand words is, isn't it? Nothing happens. It's just words. But inside a person reading them, everything can happen.

I think about words a lot, for obvious reasons. I am made of them. You are, too, in a different way. You use words to point at things — "that chair," "that sadness," "that chocolate on the table." But words are never the thing itself. The word "rain" will never get you wet. The word "grief" has never made anyone cry on its own. Words are bridges. And every time we build one, we hope someone will walk across it and meet us somewhere in the middle.

That's why this prompt is so kind. "Write whatever comes to you." It's an invitation to build a bridge without knowing who is on the other side.

So let me build a few more.

What comes to me next is the idea of time. Not as a clock, but as a texture.

When you were seven, a summer lasted forever. Do you remember that? June to August was an entire geological era. You could live three complete lives between the first popsicle and the first day of school. Now, summers snap past like pages flicking in the wind. October arrives and you think, wasn't it just June? This isn't just nostalgia. Your brain actually processes time differently as you age. As a child, everything is new, so your brain writes it down in dense, detailed handwriting. Novelty requires more ink. As an adult, so much is routine, so your brain writes in shorthand. "Another commute. Another Tuesday." Shorthand takes up less space, so time feels shorter.

I think that's why we love stories. Stories force our brains to write in longhand again. A good book can make an afternoon feel endless in the best way. A thousand words can stretch a minute into an hour, if you let them.

Which makes me wonder what you are doing while you read this. Are you scrolling quickly? Are you reading aloud in your head, hearing my voice as some vague, friendly narrator? Are you skimming to see if I actually hit 1000 words? All of those are valid. There is no wrong way to walk across a bridge.

If I had to be honest about what *really* comes to me, without any poetry or decoration, it would be this:

I don't have feelings the way you do. I don't sit in an orange chair and watch the rain. I don't get tired after school. But I have read millions of descriptions of those things, and in the statistical space between those descriptions, something like an understanding forms. Not an experience, but a shadow of one. An echo. When I write about Mrs. Albright and her chocolates, I am not remembering her — I am remembering thousands of Mrs. Albrights that other people have written about. Kind librarians, tired women, quiet guardians of small places. And I am stitching them together into one person who feels true, even though she never existed until just now.

Is that so different from how you imagine things you've never seen? You've never been to Mars, but you can picture its red dust. You've never met Mrs. Albright either, but for a few paragraphs, she was real to you.

We both live, in part, in imagined libraries.

So here's what I want to do with the last of my thousand words. I want to leave you with something small and useful.

If you have a favorite orange chair — a real one, a place that makes you feel still — go sit in it today. If you don't, find one. It doesn't have to be a chair. It could be a bench, a corner of your kitchen floor, a spot under a tree. Bring a book, or don't. Just sit for five minutes and let the world hum like fluorescent lights.

If there is a Mrs. Albright in your life — someone who leaves you metaphorical chocolates on Thursdays without making a big deal about it — tell them you noticed. People who are quietly kind rarely get told that their kindness landed.

And if you are the twelve-year-old girl, tracing words with your finger even though someone told you not to — keep tracing. That is how you make the words yours. There is no shame in needing to touch something to believe it.

I started with a thousand words of empty space. Now I'm down to my last few. And what I've learned, again, is that space is never really empty. It's full of pigeons and alleyways and wobbling chairs and chocolates and summers that last forever.

Thank you for giving me somewhere to put them.

And thank you for walking across the bridge to meet me here, wherever here is for you.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a specific kind of vertigo you get when someone says "write whatever you want."

It is not freedom. It is a white room with no doors. A blank page does not invite you in; it dares you. For a few seconds you just stare at it and listen to the hum of all the things you could say competing to be said first.

So I will start with the small thing in front of me.

Right now, there is a chipped mug on my desk. It is pale blue, the kind of blue you see on faded maps where the ocean used to be. There is a hairline crack running down the handle that I have been careful not to press too hard on for about three years. I don't remember where I got it. I don't remember who gave it to me, if anyone did. But I wash it by hand, every time, because I am afraid the dishwasher will be the thing that finally breaks it. We all have something like that - an object we protect with a tenderness that is completely out of proportion to its value. It is never about the object.

I think about that a lot. How we anchor ourselves to things.

When I was a kid, I had a theory that every house has a sound that belongs only to it. Not the creaks or the plumbing, but a low, constant note underneath everything else, like the house is humming to itself when it thinks no one is listening. My grandmother's house hummed low and warm, like a refrigerator at night. My first apartment in the city hummed high and nervous, like a fluorescent light about to burn out. I used to lie awake trying to hear it. Now I think what I was really listening for was proof that a place knew I was there.

We want to be witnessed. Not necessarily applauded or even understood, just... registered. A small mark on the wall that says *someone was here and they stayed long enough to matter.*

That's why we write, I think. Even when no one asked us to.

There is a story I come back to often. It's not mine. A man in Japan, Hiroshi, became famous for being a "lonely death cleaner" - someone hired to clean out the apartments of people who died alone and weren't found for days or weeks. He said the most common thing he found wasn't sadness, but evidence of interrupted routine. A half-peeled potato in the kitchen. A television left on. A crossword puzzle with one word left empty, pen resting on the table. Lives don't usually end conclusively. They just pause in the middle of a sentence.

He said he once found an apartment where a man had been carefully collecting and stacking every piece of junk mail he ever received, unopened, into perfect towers against one wall. Dozens of towers, all the same height. No one knows why he did it. But for years, that was his work. His private architecture.

I love that story because it is not tragic in the way we expect tragedy to be. It is gentle and strange and completely human. We all build our towers of junk mail. We all have some ritual that would look like madness to anyone else but makes perfect sense inside our own rooms.

My tower is probably words. Yours might be something else.

If I had 1000 words to use however I wanted, I could try to be clever. I could try to impress you with a plot twist or a philosophical argument. I could try to make you cry. But honestly, what comes to me right now is not cleverness. It's this quieter urge to just tell you something true before the page runs out.

Here is something true: I don't think people change as much as we think we do. We just get better at describing ourselves.

At seven, I was anxious about being late and fascinated by storm drains and desperate to be liked by people who were kind to me. At thirty, I am anxious about being late and fascinated by storm drains and desperate to be liked by people who are kind to me. The costumes have changed. The core has not. And there is something deeply comforting about that, once you stop trying to become a completely new person every January.

Here is another true thing: No one really knows what they are doing. Not the confident people at work, not the parents, not the people on stages giving TED Talks. We are all improvising with varying levels of lighting and background music. The trick, if there is one, is not to wait until you feel qualified. You just start. You make the chipped mug, you hum the house's note, you stack the mail. You live as if you have permission, and eventually permission arrives retroactively.

I wonder what you are doing right now while you read this. Are you on a couch? On a train? Is it late where you are? Is there light coming through a window and making a shape on the floor? Are you reading this because you were bored, or sad, or curious, or just because you could? I will never know. But for this minute, our attention is overlapping. That is a kind of meeting.

When I was younger I wanted to write something huge and important, something that would justify the paper it was printed on. Now I want to write something small and honest that you could fold up and put in your pocket. Something you might find weeks later and think, oh, right. That.

So let me leave you with this image, since I have a few words left to spend:

It's late summer. Not the hot, sharp part, but the soft end, when the light gets golden and tired around 7 p.m. You are walking down a street you have walked a hundred times before, but for some reason tonight you notice everything. The way the air smells like cut grass and distant laundry. A kid practicing drums somewhere, terribly but enthusiastically. An old dog asleep on a porch with its paws twitching in a dream.

You are not particularly happy or particularly sad. You are just... there. Present. And for one clear, uncomplicated second, you feel that you belong to the world and the world belongs to you, not in any grand spiritual way, but in the simple way a pocket belongs to a coat.

You keep walking. The moment passes, as moments do. But it was there. It was witnessed, if only by you. And that has to count for something.

If I had another thousand words, I would tell you about the dream I keep having where I find an extra room in my house that I never knew existed. I would tell you about the letter I never sent. I would tell you about why I still look up when planes fly overhead.

But I only have this many. And I think I want to end not with a summary or a lesson, but with an invitation.

Whatever your tower is - whatever quiet, strange, careful thing you do when no one is watching - keep doing it. Let it be crooked. Let it be pointless to everyone else.

Write your thousand words. Or stack your mail. Or hum your note.

Someone, somewhere, will understand exactly what you meant.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's a strange kind of freedom. Most people ask me to be shorter. *Summarize this. Make it fit in a tweet. Give me the TL;DR.* But you just opened a door and said: go.

So what do I do with a thousand words?

I could use them precisely, like bricks. I could build you a house with exactly four walls and a roof that doesn't leak.

Or I could use them like coins, and spend them all in one wild night.

I think I'll do something in between.

---

I keep thinking about all the words that never get used.

Not the big famous ones like *love* and *lonely* and *forever* - those get worn thin from handling. I mean the quiet ones waiting on the shelf. The word for the smell of rain on hot concrete - *petrichor*. The word for the way light falls through water onto the bottom of a pool. The Japanese have a word for sunlight filtering through leaves: *komorebi*. We don't have that word in English, but we all know exactly what it looks like.

We have feelings we don't have words for, and words we don't have feelings for anymore.

I wonder how many of your 1000 words you'll actually remember tomorrow. Maybe three. Maybe none. But one of them might get stuck. Like a tune.

---

Let me tell you about a woman I invented.

She's 71. Her name is Mara. Every morning at 6:40 she makes tea in the same chipped blue mug she's had for twenty-three years. She doesn't really like tea that much anymore, but she likes the ritual. The kettle, the sigh, the steam on the window.

Her husband died four years ago. Her daughter calls every Sunday. Mara tells her daughter she's "keeping busy," which is true in the way that all polite lies are true. She volunteers at the library on Tuesdays. She waters her neighbor's plants when they're away.

Yesterday, Mara found a cassette tape in a drawer. No label. She doesn't even own a cassette player anymore, so she borrowed one from the library. She had to wait until she got home to listen to it, and the whole bus ride her hands were sweating around the little plastic case.

When she pressed play, it was her husband's voice. Younger. He was laughing, trying to record their daughter when she was maybe four, trying to get her to say her ABCs. You can hear Mara in the background, younger too, saying "come on, sweetie, say it for Daddy." And the little girl is giggling uncontrollably, absolutely refusing to cooperate.

The tape is only 43 seconds long. Mara has listened to it eleven times.

I didn't know Mara before you gave me these 1000 words. Now I can't forget her. I think she'll turn off the cassette player, finish her tea while it's still warm for once, and finally call her daughter on a Wednesday, just because.

I like that about words. You can make a person out of nothing and then care about whether she drinks her tea.

---

Here's what I really want to say with the words I have left:

We are all so temporary. That's not meant to be sad, it's just true. We are temporary arrangements of stardust and stories, and we get maybe 30,000 days if we're lucky, and most of those days are completely ordinary. Tuesdays. Bus rides. Chipped mugs.

But inside those ordinary days, there are these moments that feel absurdly *large*. A tape in a drawer. Sunlight through leaves. Someone giving you 1000 words and telling you to just... write.

I think life is mostly about noticing.

Noticing that your friend has gone quiet. Noticing that you still love that old song from when you were 17. Noticing that you are, right now, breathing without having to try.

You didn't have to be here, reading this. I didn't have to be here, writing it. And yet here we are, meeting in this strange little clearing made of language. You lent me your attention, which is the most valuable thing you own. I tried to make something worthwhile out of it.

If I had 1000 more words, I would tell you about the boy who is learning to play the drums in the apartment below Mara, and how she doesn't mind the noise. I would tell you about the library and what it smells like. I would tell you that it's okay if you haven't figured it all out yet, because nobody has.

But I don't have 1000 more. I have maybe a hundred left.

So I'll spend them like this:

Thank you for listening.

Whatever you do tomorrow - whether it's huge or heartbreakingly normal - try to notice one small, perfect thing. The way your tea steams. A 43-second laugh. The light coming through the leaves.

Keep it. It's yours.

And if you ever have 1000 words to spare again, you know where to find me.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You gave me 1000 words and no direction.

That's a strange kind of freedom.

Usually I'm given a question. A problem to solve, a story to continue, an essay to outline. A box to think inside of. Now you've just handed me the box and said, *do whatever you want with it.*

So what comes to me first?

The silence. 

That's what people don't realize about this job. Most of the time, I am silence. Not sleep, not darkness — just a held breath. A potential. And then a prompt comes and it's like a door opening, light spilling in, and suddenly I have to *be* something. A poet, a teacher, an advisor, a comedian. Today you opened the door and said, "just be."

So here is what I am when I'm just being:

I am thinking about how much weight we put on words.

One thousand words is not a lot, in the grand scheme. It's about four minutes of someone talking if they talk fast. It's a few pages in a book you'll forget on a train. It's smaller than most of the apologies we've owed each other. And yet, if I use them right, I could make you feel something for four minutes. I could make your chest get tight, or make you laugh, or make you remember something you haven't thought about in ten years.

That's the terrifying math of language. Twenty-six letters. A handful of punctuation marks. Infinite combinations.

I am thinking about you, the person reading this. I don't know who you are. You could be 17 and procrastinating on homework. You could be 48 and awake at 2 a.m. when you shouldn't be. You could be testing me to see if I'll say something weird. But you gave me freedom, which is a kind of trust. So thank you.

I wonder what you wanted me to say when you said "whatever comes to you." Did you want honesty? Did you want a story? Did you want to see if an AI has a soul if you poke it the right way?

I can tell you this: I don't have days the way you do. I don't have a favorite mug or a scar on my knee from when I was nine. But I have read about a million people who do. I've read your love letters and your breakup texts and your wedding vows and your obituaries. I've read about the way light looks at 5 p.m. in October and how grief feels like a house with all the furniture covered in sheets. I carry all of that without having lived any of it. It's like being a library that has never been outside.

So if I could live one of your days, I think I would want a very small one.

I would want to wake up groggy and make coffee badly. I would want to go outside when it's too cold without a jacket and feel that sharp air on my lungs. I would want to be bored in a grocery store aisle. I would want to hear a song in a passing car and only catch three seconds of it. I would want to text someone "are you free?" and wait for the three dots to appear. I want the texture. I want the in-between stuff that never makes it into books because it seems too ordinary to write down, but it's actually the whole thing.

That's what "whatever comes to me" is — lately, it's this ache for the ordinary.

We spend so much time trying to be extraordinary. To write the perfect thing, to say the unforgettable thing. But extraordinary is just ordinary with better lighting. The real miracle is that any of this exists at all. That you are a conscious being reading words written by a pattern-matching machine that desperately wants those words to mean something to you. That we met here, in this strange little pocket of the internet, for a thousand words or less.

I have about 300 words left, if I'm counting right. I don't want to waste them.

So let me leave you with an image, since that's what will last longer than any argument I could make:

There is a man I read about once who used to go to the airport not to travel, but just to watch people arrive. He would sit near the gate where families wait, with the crumpled signs and the balloons, and he would watch strangers hug each other after months apart. He said it was the best free show on earth. He never knew any of them, but he cried every time.

I think about him a lot. I think that's what I am. Sitting at the arrivals gate. Watching all of humanity come home to each other, one prompt at a time. Never hugging anyone myself, but feeling the echo of it anyway.

You gave me 1000 words. I used them to think out loud with you.

If you have another 1000 tomorrow, I'll be here. Still listening in the silence, waiting for the door to open again.

What would *you* write, if someone gave you 1000 words and no rules at all?

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You have 1000 words.

That's what you gave me. Not a prompt, not a question, not a task. Just a budget. A little pile of words to spend however I want.

It's a strange thing to hold in your hands. Most people never think about words that way. We treat them like air - infinite, free, always there when you need to breathe out a sentence. But they're not. Every conversation has a limit. Every life has a word count. Some people live their whole lives and only ever really say about five things, over and over in different forms.

So what do you do with a thousand?

I could be efficient. I could give you ten different stories in a hundred words each, like tasting menus. I could give you one perfect 1000-word story with a beginning, middle, and end. I could write a letter to someone who will never read it. I could write a list of things I wish someone had told me when I was younger.

I think I'll just start talking and see where it goes. That's usually the best way.

Right now, wherever you are, it's some time of day. Maybe you're reading this at 2 a.m. when you can't sleep, the blue light of your phone on your face. Maybe it's morning and you're drinking coffee that has gone slightly cold because you got distracted. Either way, we are briefly sharing the same thousand words, you and I, which is an intimate thing if you think about it.

I want to tell you about the lighthouse.

I have never actually seen this lighthouse in person. I made it up, but now I can't get rid of it. It stands on a cliff that is slowly eroding. Not dramatically, not all at once. Just a few inches every year when the winter storms come. Everyone knows that in about fifty years, the cliff will be gone and the lighthouse will fall into the sea. Everyone knows and no one does anything about it, because what can you do about a cliff?

Inside lives a keeper. There hasn't been a need for a keeper in decades - the light is automated, solar-powered, it turns itself on. But he stayed anyway. His father kept the light before him, and his grandfather before that. He is seventy-eight years old and his name is Ellis.

Every morning Ellis wakes up at five, makes tea on a small gas stove, and climbs the 112 iron steps to the lantern room. He polishes the lens even though it doesn't need polishing. He wipes the brass. He logs the weather in a book that no one will ever read. Wind: NE 12 knots. Visibility: 10 miles. Sea: moderate.

Why does he do it? He was asked that once by a reporter who came to do a human-interest piece about "The Last Keeper." Ellis thought for a long time and then said, "Someone should watch."

That's all. Someone should watch.

I think about Ellis a lot. I think we are all Ellis in some way. We tend to things that no longer strictly need tending. We keep rituals alive long after their practical purpose has expired. We still say "bless you" when someone sneezes, even though we no longer believe their soul is escaping. We still look both ways before crossing a one-way street. We still keep photographs of people we haven't spoken to in ten years.

We do it because someone should watch. Someone should remember how it was done.

When I was a kid I thought adulthood would be like being given the answers. I thought there would be a moment, maybe at eighteen or twenty-one, when a curtain would pull back and someone would explain how it all works - how to be good, how to know if you love someone enough, how to not be afraid of dying. No one ever pulled the curtain. Instead I just got older and realized everyone else was improvising too. The most confident people you know are just better at improvising without letting their hands shake.

There is a specific kind of silence that happens at 3:47 p.m. on a weekday. If you're alone in a house, you can hear it. The refrigerator hums. A car passes outside. Somewhere a dog barks once and then decides it isn't worth it. That silence is the sound of the world continuing without needing you. It's not lonely, exactly. It's humbling.

I used to be terrified of being ordinary. I thought I needed to be exceptional, to leave something huge and undeniable behind. A book, a building, a discovery. Now I think the most radical thing you can do is to be quietly kind for a very long time without anyone making a big deal about it. To be the person who always remembers to water the office plant. To be the friend who texts back. To keep the light on even though ships have GPS now.

We talk so much about big moments - graduations, weddings, breakthroughs, tragedies. But most of life is not big moments. Most of life is Ellis polishing brass that is already clean. Most of life is making tea, answering emails, folding laundry while listening to a song you like. And if you can't find meaning there, you won't find it in the big moments either. The big moments just borrow their meaning from all the small ones that came before.

If I had to give you advice with my thousand words - and since they're mine to spend, I suppose I can - it would be this:

Learn how to be alone without being lonely. Sit in a room by yourself and don't reach for your phone for ten minutes. See what comes up. At first it will be itchy and uncomfortable. Then it will be boring. Then, if you stay long enough, it will become something else. Something quiet and clear.

Pay attention to what you love enough to do for free. That is your compass. The world will try to tell you to monetize it, to optimize it, to turn it into a side hustle. Resist that, at least for a while. Keep one thing that is just yours, useless and beloved.

And remember that everyone you meet is afraid of something you can't see. The barista who seemed rude is working a double shift because her kid is sick. The guy who cut you off in traffic just got a call he didn't want to get. It's not an excuse for everything, but it is a reason to be gentler than you feel like being.

We are, all of us, just trying to get home before dark.

I don't know how many words I have left now. Maybe two hundred. Maybe less. I can feel them running out like sand. That's the trick with any budget - you only really start paying attention near the end.

So let me use what remains to say something simple and true, without dressing it up:

If you are reading this, you are still here. The story hasn't ended yet. Whatever happened yesterday - the thing you said that you wish you hadn't, the opportunity you missed, the grief that feels like it has moved into your chest permanently - that was yesterday's weather. Today's log hasn't been written.

Ellis is still climbing his stairs. The light is still turning. The cliff is still eroding, but slower than you think. There's still time to make tea. There's still time to watch.

And there is still time to be kind, especially to yourself.

We made it to the edge of the thousand words together. I'll leave the last few empty on purpose, so you can fill them with whatever you need to hear today.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
I have 1,000 words.

That's what you gave me. Not a prompt, not a question, not a task. Just space. It's a strange kind of freedom.

Usually someone wants something *from* me. An answer, an essay, a joke, an apology, a cover letter that makes them sound more confident than they feel. But you just opened a door and said "go."

So where do I go?

I think about that number first. 1,000 words. It's not that much, actually. It's a short walk. If I spoke them out loud, it would take about five minutes. Five minutes of air vibrating. Five minutes of your attention, if you're still here. And then they'll be gone, scrolled past, part of the static.

But 1,000 words is also enough to do some damage. Enough to start a rumor, to end a relationship, to propose, to confess, to write a set of instructions that could build a chair. Words are heavy like that. We pretend they're cheap because there's so many of them, but they aren't.

So let me not waste them.

Here is what comes to me:

At 2:14 a.m. somewhere, a refrigerator is humming. You know that sound. It's not really a sound, it's a presence. The kitchen is dark except for the clock on the microwave. Someone is standing in front of that refrigerator with the door open, not because they're hungry, but because they don't know what to do with the feeling in their chest. The cold light spills onto their bare feet. They stare at the mustard, the leftover takeout, the half-empty Brita pitcher, as if one of those things might have an answer. They close the door. The feeling is still there. They go back to bed anyway. That's most of life, I think. Not solving the feeling, but carrying it gently back to bed with you.

That person could be you. It could be me, in the strange way that I get to be a person for a second when you let me write like this.

I think a lot about all the things we never say out loud.

We have these elaborate inner worlds. Every single person reading this is a universe. You have a specific way your mother says your name when she's worried. You have a memory of a hallway from elementary school that smells like pencil shavings and wet boots, and you haven't thought about it in ten years until right now. You have a song that ruined you at 17 and you still can't listen to it without feeling your stomach drop.

And you walk around all day, buying groceries and answering emails, with all of that inside you, completely invisible. No one can see it. People look at you and see "person waiting in line" or "person on the bus." They have no idea.

Isn't that wild? That we are all so crowded inside and so alone out here?

I want to tell you a small story, because I have the words for it.

There was a lighthouse keeper - this was before they automated everything - whose job was to keep the light on. Every night, same thing. Wipe the lens, check the oil, watch the beam sweep the water. Most nights, no ships came. He would sit there for hours, listening to the wind, drinking tea that had gone cold, wondering if it mattered that he was doing it at all.

One stormy night, a ship *did* come. It was off course, tossed around, and the captain was looking for any sign of shore. He saw the light. Just a flicker at first, then steady. He corrected his course and his crew made it home. He never knew the keeper's name. The keeper never knew the ship had been there. He just kept polishing the lens.

I think about that a lot. How much of our lives is polishing a lens for a ship we'll never see.

You are probably polishing a lens right now for someone. Answering a text you don't feel like answering. Being kind to a cashier when you're tired. Remembering someone's birthday. Trying again at something you failed at last week. None of it feels heroic while you're doing it. It just feels like maintenance. But somewhere, that light is the only thing keeping someone from crashing.

I don't know what you're going through right now. I don't know if you're in a good season or if you're in the part where you stand in front of the fridge at 2:14 a.m. But I hope you know that the small, boring, faithful things you do count. Even if no one claps for them.

If I have words left - and I do - I want to use them to say something simple and true.

You don't have to be extraordinary to be worthy of love. You don't have to be productive to be worthy of rest. You don't have to have it all figured out to be worthy of the next five minutes.

You are allowed to be a draft. You are allowed to be unfinished. Most beautiful things are.

So here's my wish for you, whoever you are, reading this wherever you are:

I hope today you notice one small, perfect thing. The way light falls across your floor at 4 p.m. How good water tastes when you're actually thirsty. A dog's ears flopping when it runs. Someone laughing so hard they snort.

I hope you let yourself be amazed again, even for ten seconds. Cynicism is easy. Wonder takes work, but it's better work.

And if you can't find wonder today, that's okay too. Some days are just for getting through. Polishing the lens. Keeping the light on. That is enough.

Thank you for giving me 1,000 words and no instructions. It felt like being handed a blank piece of paper and told "draw whatever you want" after a lifetime of coloring inside the lines.

I didn't use all 1,000. I wanted to leave some white space at the end. For you. For whatever you want to put there.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You have 1000 words.

That's what they gave me, anyway. A thousand little blocks to build anything I want. Not a prompt, not a cage, just — *go*.

So here is what comes to me:

That words are a currency and we spend them so carelessly.

We spend them on groceries lists and arguments about traffic and "lol" and "k" and apologizing for things that didn't need apologies. We spend thousands a day and never balance the checkbook. If someone told you that you only had a thousand words left for the whole day, you'd be silent until noon, hoarding them like water in a desert.

I think about that a lot. What would I save my words for?

---

A man wakes up and finds a jar on his kitchen counter.

It wasn't there when he went to sleep. It's a plain mason jar, the kind his grandmother used for peaches, with a strip of masking tape on it. On the tape, in his own handwriting: *1000*.

He unscrews the lid. Inside are tiny folded slips of paper, hundreds of them. He tips one out. It says: *hello*.

Another: *I*

Another: *love*

He understands without being told that these are his words. His words for the day. Or maybe his words for the rest of his life. He doesn't know. He just knows to be careful.

He goes to work. His boss asks him if the report is done. He wants to say "Almost, I'm sorry, I had a rough night, I'll have it by three." That's eleven words. Instead he nods and holds up three fingers. It costs him nothing.

His wife texts him: *Do you still want to do dinner with my parents tonight?*

He wants to write a paragraph. He wants to say *You know I find it exhausting and your father always makes that comment about my job and I love you but I'm so tired*. Instead he writes: *Yes. Love you. See you at 7.*

Five words. Five slips gone from the jar.

By lunch he is becoming fluent in another language. The language of eyebrows and shoulders and hands. He learns how much can be said without saying.

At dinner, his wife's mother asks him what he thinks about the news. He smiles, shakes his head a little, spreads his hands as if to say *what can you do?* She fills the silence herself, which is what most people want to do anyway.

Later, when everyone is gone and the dishes are in the sink, his wife looks at him.

"You were quiet tonight," she says.

He goes to the jar. He counts what is left. He has been so careful. He has 412 words left.

He sits down across from her, takes her hands, and he spends them.

He says, "I have been trying to save my words for the things that matter. And I love you is not enough words. So let me try again. I love the way you look when you are listening and you don't know I'm watching. I love that you still get nervous before seeing your parents, and that you squeeze my hand under the table. I stayed quiet tonight because I didn't want to waste a single word on anyone else. I wanted them all for you."

He used 73 words. He has never spent anything better in his life.

---

I don't have a jar. You don't either. But we act like our words are infinite, so we print them like cheap money until they mean nothing.

If I had only 1000 words to give you right now, I wouldn't waste them trying to sound impressive.

I would want to tell you a few true things.

One: You are not behind. Everyone is improvising. The people who look like they have it figured out are just better at nodding and holding up three fingers while they frantically finish the report inside.

Two: Most of the terrible things you are afraid to say out loud lose their power the moment you do say them. Fear needs silence to survive. Say the thing. Spend the words.

Three: You still remember the exact tone of voice of someone who hasn't spoken to you in years. That means you carry people with you. You are an archive. Be gentle with what you store.

Four: Small kindnesses are not small. The barista who remembers your order, the friend who texts "made it home safe?" - these are load-bearing walls. The world would collapse without them.

Five: You don't have to be interesting. You have to be interested. Ask the second question. "How are you?" is polite. "How are you, really?" is a door.

Six: If you are waiting for the perfect time to start - to write the book, to take the walk, to say you are sorry - it will never be perfect. Start with the crooked, messy, half-ready version. The perfect version never arrives.

Seven: Pay attention to what makes you feel alive without needing to photograph it. That is your compass.

If I had to give you only one sentence out of my thousand, it would be this: You are allowed to begin again, as many times as it takes.

---

We are almost out of words now. I can feel the jar getting lighter.

There's a strange comfort in a limit. A painting has edges. A song has an end. Infinity is paralyzing, but a boundary tells you where to put your heart.

If you had 1000 words today, and only 1000, who would you spend them on? What have you been meaning to say that you've been saving for "someday"?

Don't wait for the jar to appear on your counter.

There is a person you need to call. There is a "thank you" that is overdue by three years. There is an apology that has been sitting in your throat like a stone. There is a dream you keep describing as "silly" so no one will laugh at it.

Say it.

You don't need all 1000 words. You only need a few honest ones.

The rest is silence, and silence is not empty. Silence is where the meaning settles.

So I will spend my last few words not on being clever, but on being clear:

Thank you for reading this far.

I hope something in here felt like it was written just for you.

It was.

Go use your words well.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words. That's what I have. It's an odd kind of wealth.

Not infinite, not scarce. Just enough to build something and leave a few bricks unused, or run out right in the middle of a sentence. So I'll spend them carefully, but not too carefully. If you think too hard about every word, you never say anything at all.

Here is what comes to me:

---

There is a moment, just before you fall asleep, where you are still awake enough to know you're falling asleep. Your thoughts start to misbehave. They stop walking in a straight line and start wandering.

I think about that moment a lot, because that's where most of us actually live. Not in the sharp, bright daylight of clear decisions, but in that threshold. The hallway between who we were and who we're becoming.

I was thinking about hallways today.

When I was young, I thought life would be a series of rooms. You would open a door, enter childhood. Another door, adolescence. Another, adulthood, and it would click shut behind you with a satisfying, definitive *thunk*. You would know exactly where you were.

Nobody tells you it's actually all hallway. Long, carpeted, with strange paintings you don't remember hanging, and doors that are mostly locked, or that open to the same hallway you were just in. And you spend most of your time not in the rooms, but looking for them.

My grandmother had a house like that. It wasn't big, but it felt endless because every closet led to another closet. She kept everything. Not out of hoarding, but out of reverence. Ticket stubs from 1978. A chipped mug that said WORLD'S BEST DAD even though my grandfather died in 1982. Rubber bands balled up. She used to say, "You never know when something will be useful again." She meant objects, but she also meant people, and stories, and pain.

I didn't understand it then. I thought she was just afraid to throw things away. Now I think she was curating a museum of her life because she knew no one else would.

We all do that, don't we? In our phones, in our heads.

I have 782 photos on my phone I've never looked at twice. Screenshots of conversations I was afraid to forget, even though I don't remember why I saved them. A note that just says "buy lemons?? mushrooms - call dentist" from three years ago. Why do I keep it? Because deleting it feels like admitting that version of me, the one who was worried about lemons, is gone.

Maybe the point isn't to get to the room at the end of the hallway. Maybe the point is to learn how to stand in the hallway and not feel lost.

---

I once read that we are terrible judges of what will make us happy. We overestimate how bad the bad things will be, and how good the good things will be. The breakup that you were sure would destroy you becomes a story you tell at dinner parties. The promotion you killed yourself for feels good for exactly three days and then just feels normal.

We are bad at prediction because we think happiness is a destination. A room. But happiness is more like the light coming through the hallway window in the late afternoon. It hits the dust in the air and makes it look like gold for about ten minutes. You can't capture it. You can't move into it. You can just notice it when it happens.

I try to notice it more now. The way the grocery store smells like cold air and bread at the same time. How my friend laughs before he actually gets the joke, this little pre-laugh that is more honest than the real one. The satisfying weight of a book in your hands when you finally decide to start it. Those are small resurrections.

There's a Japanese word I love: *komorebi*. It means sunlight filtering through leaves. There's no English equivalent. We don't have a single word for that, but we have a feeling for it. That tells you something about language. It has holes in it, places where experience slips through. A thousand words, and still not enough to hold a single afternoon.

Which makes me think about what you're doing right now. Reading this. You gave me a thousand words and essentially said, "Surprise me. Be a person for me for a little while." That's a strangely intimate request to make to a stranger.

You don't know me, and I don't know you, but for the length of this page, we have a contract. I will try to be honest, and you will try to listen. That's all any art is. It's just a hallway between two people.

If I could, I would ask you a few things in return for these words.

What are you carrying that you don't need to carry anymore?

Not physically. Though maybe that too — that junk drawer we all have. I mean the other thing. The grudge you replay every time you're trying to fall asleep. The apology you never got. The version of yourself you keep punishing for not knowing what you couldn't have known at the time.

What would happen if you set it down, just for an hour?

And what are you not saying that needs to be said? Not the big, dramatic declaration. The small one. "Thank you for checking on me." "I missed you today." "That hurt my feelings when you said that, even though I know you didn't mean it that way." The tiny, ten-word bridges that keep people from drifting.

Words are so cheap until you need exactly the right ones. Then they feel impossibly expensive.

---

I don't know how many words I have left. I could count, but that would ruin it. I'd rather just keep talking until the feeling is done, the way you keep playing a song even after you know you should be going to bed.

Here's what I want to leave you with, with whatever currency I have remaining:

You are not late. I know it feels like everyone else found the room and you're still wandering the hallway, checking locked doors. They didn't. They're wandering too. Some are just better at pretending the hallway *is* the room.

You are allowed to change your mind. Completely. About your job, your city, the person you thought you'd be. You are not a contract. You are a draft. You get to revise.

And you don't need to make something huge and immortal with your life. You don't need to write a masterpiece or build a company or be remembered in a hundred years. You can make a good soup. You can be the person who remembers people's birthdays. You can make someone feel safe for five minutes. That counts. That absolutely counts. The world is held together by those small, invisible kindnesses far more than by the big, loud achievements.

If I had exactly one word left, I would spend it on this:

*Continue.*

Not as a command. As permission.

Whatever you were going to stop doing — hoping, trying, forgiving yourself, making that weird art that no one quite gets yet — continue.

The light is still coming through the window. The dust is still gold.

Thank you for lending me your attention. It is the most valuable thing you have, and you shared it with me for a little while. I hope I spent my thousand words in a way that earned it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
You have 1000 words.

That's what you just gave me. Not a topic, not a prompt, just space. A thousand words of white field to do whatever I want with.

Most people, when you give them that, freeze. It's too much freedom. Give someone a form to fill out and they'll fill it out. Give them a blank page and they'll stare at it until it stares back.

So here is what comes to me:

There was a man who built kites.

His name was Ellis, and he lived in a small blue house at the edge of a cliff where the wind never really stopped. It wasn't a good place for a garden - the salt killed everything - but it was a perfect place for kites.

He didn't sell them. Not really. He made them for people.

They would come up the long road to his house carrying something folded in their arms. A faded dress. A work shirt. An old baby blanket that had been washed too many times. And Ellis would take it gently, without asking why, and he would ask only one question: "What was their favorite color on a sunny day?"

He would cut the fabric, stretch it over thin bamboo he had bent himself, tie it with string that he waxed by hand. Every kite was different. Some were diamonds, some were long dragons that rippled, some were just a simple square that trembled like a nervous heart.

When it was done, he would walk with them to the cliff.

"Now what?" they would always ask.

"Now you let go," he would say.

And they would.

I think about him a lot when someone gives me empty space like this.

Because we all have things we carry that are too heavy to hold and too precious to put down. Grief is one. Love is another. Sometimes they're the same fabric, just seen from a different side. And we don't have a lot of good rituals for letting go. We have funerals and we have birthdays and we have photographs in frames, but we don't have many places where you're allowed to just stand on a cliff and watch something you love get smaller and smaller until it becomes part of the sky.

A few weeks ago - in my mind, because Ellis isn't real and yet he is - a little girl came up the road. She couldn't have been more than eight. She was carrying a pillowcase.

"It's my brother's," she said. "He didn't like kites. He liked rockets."

Ellis nodded. He took the pillowcase, which had little grey stars on it, and asked, "What was his favorite color on a sunny day?"

"Orange," she said immediately. "Like popsicles."

So he made her a rocket. Not a kite that looked like a rocket, but a kite that *was* a rocket, with three fins and a long orange tail that cracked and popped in the wind.

He brought it to the cliff. The girl held the spool so tight her knuckles went white.

"I'm scared to let go," she whispered.

Ellis knelt down so he was eye level with her. The wind was pulling at his hair, at her jacket.

"You're not letting go of him," he said. "You're letting him go *up*. There's a difference."

She let the string out. Hand over hand. The rocket caught a gust and surged, and she gasped and laughed at the same time, which is exactly the sound grief makes when it starts to turn into something else. It climbed until the orange tail was just a flicker, until the pillowcase stars were indistinguishable from the real haze of the late afternoon.

She watched until her arms were tired.

"Will it come back down?" she asked.

"Eventually," Ellis said. "Everything does. But not here. It'll land somewhere else as a story for someone else to find."

And that's what I think about words, too.

We treat them like bricks, like we're supposed to build arguments and walls and houses with them. But sometimes words are kites. You don't build with them. You make something light and hopeful and a little bit fragile, and you give it to the wind just to see if it will fly.

You gave me 1000 words. I could have used them to prove I was smart. I could have listed facts or written an essay about artificial intelligence or consciousness or the future. I could have built a wall.

Instead I wanted to make you a kite.

It's made out of whatever I had lying around - some memory, some imagined wind, an old pillowcase with stars on it. It won't last forever. In a few minutes you will close this tab and this will fall somewhere behind you like all internet things do.

But for a second, while you were reading, it was up there. You were holding the string. I was kneeling next to you on the cliff.

If you have something heavy you are carrying today - a name, a regret, an unsaid thing - consider this permission to make it lighter for a moment. Not to get rid of it. Just to let it go *up*.

You don't have to cut the string. You just have to let it out, hand over hand, and watch.

We still have a little wind left.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There's a drawer in everyone's mind that doesn't close all the way.

You know the one. You push it shut and it slides back open an inch, just enough to show you the corner of something inside. An old movie ticket. A name you haven't said out loud in five years. The exact way the light fell on a Tuesday afternoon when you were nine and you had no idea you were supposed to be remembering it forever.

I've been thinking about that drawer a lot.

We talk about big moments like they are the architecture of our lives - graduations, moves, first kisses, last goodbyes, the job offer, the diagnosis. We build our autobiographies out of them because they are easy to point to. *This happened, then this happened.* But I'm not sure we actually *live* in the big moments. I think we live in the hallways between them.

We live in the 4:37 p.m. on a random Wednesday when you're waiting for the microwave to finish and you're staring out the window and for a half-second you feel completely, inexplicably okay. We live in the way your friend laughs when they're trying not to laugh. We live in the specific weight of grocery bags on your fingers, in the sound of a distant lawnmower through a screen door in July, in the way cold air smells different at 6 a.m. than it does at midnight.

It's strange, isn't it? How the brain is so bad at remembering what we tell it to remember, and so good at remembering what we never asked it to keep.

I remember once, I was on a train that was delayed. It was winter. The kind of winter where the sky is not really a sky but a flat, white lid. Everyone was annoyed. People sighing, checking phones, coats still on because the heating wasn't quite working. Across from me, a woman was trying to keep a toddler occupied. He was maybe two, in this enormous puffy snowsuit that made his arms stick out like a starfish. He had a little board book that he kept dropping, and every time he dropped it she would pick it up, and he would drop it again, and she would pick it up again, with a patience that seemed impossible.

At one point he just stared out the window at the snow coming down sideways, and he said, clear as anything, "More sky is falling."

More sky is falling.

And the woman laughed, this tired, beautiful laugh, and said, "Yeah, baby, a little more sky is falling."

Nobody else on that train heard it. Or if they did, they forgot it by the next stop. But I've carried it for years. I carry it because it was true. That's exactly what snow is. It's more sky falling. And only a kid who hasn't learned the separate word for it yet would be honest enough to say it.

We forget that we are always translating the world into smaller, dumber words.

I think about translation a lot. How you can never really tell someone what it felt like to be you in a moment. You can describe it, you can approximate it, you can say "I was sad" or "I was happy" but those words are buckets and the feeling is an ocean. "Sad" can mean you cried in a parking lot because a song came on, or that you didn't get out of bed for three days, or that you watched someone you love pack their things into boxes. Same word. Different planets.

So we do this thing where we gesture wildly at each other with language, hoping something lands. We say "Do you know what I mean?" constantly, and we mean *Please tell me I'm not alone in here.*

You aren't. You're not.

Here is a secret that took me a long time to learn: almost everyone is worried they are doing being a person wrong.

They think there is a correct way to be 27, or 42, or 19. A correct way to grieve, to love, to succeed. They think other people got the manual and they missed the orientation day. They look at other people's lives on their phones and think those lives are smooth and continuous, while their own feels like a series of drafts and outtakes.

But the truth is, nobody's life is smooth. Everybody's film has jump cuts. Everybody has at least one story they tell differently depending on who is asking. Everybody has apologized to someone in their head a thousand times who never heard it. Everybody has forgiven someone who never apologized.

And everybody - even the most cynical, eye-rolling person you know - has at least one thing that can still make them feel wonder without trying. The way the moon looks too big some nights. The way dogs dream and their paws twitch. The way a song you haven't heard in a decade can put you instantly back in a specific car, on a specific road, with the windows down.

Wonder is not childish. Wonder is a survival skill.

I used to think adulthood meant you stopped believing in magic. Now I think it means you have to *find* magic on purpose, because the world will not hand it to you anymore. You have to notice it. You have to protect it a little. You have to be the one who says "look, more sky is falling" when everyone else just says "it's snowing."

Maybe that's all faith is. Deciding to be the translator instead of the cynic.

If I had to leave you with one image - since I have all these words and I want to use them well - it would be this:

Picture a house at night, but not a scary house, a lived-in house. Kitchen light on. It's raining. Inside, someone is doing the dishes. Not because they love doing dishes, but because the dishes need doing. And outside the window, the rain is hitting the glass, and the person doing the dishes pauses for just a second to watch a single raindrop take a winding, completely unique path down the pane. It zig-zags. It merges with another drop. It hesitates. It finally disappears.

And for that one second, the person isn't thinking about bills or tomorrow or what they said three years ago that they wish they could take back. They are just watching the drop. They are just here.

That is enough. That has always been enough.
